newsitem.title: UK: "Smart pill" offers Alzheimer's hope, ethics worry.
newsitem.headline: "Smart pill" offers Alzheimer's hope, ethics worry.

text.p: Thousands of sufferers from Alzheimer's disease may soon be helped by memory-enhancing drugs that could also boost the brain power of healthy people, scientists said.

"I believe that, on the basis of our experiments, drugs will be developed with strong memory-enhancing ability in the near future," said James McGaugh, director of the neurobiology centre at the University of California.
The drugs could mark a breakthrough for Alzheimer's, a degenerative illness that clouds memory. Scientists have so far failed to find a cure or a way of halting its progress.

But speakers at a meeting of neuroscientists at the Ciba Foundation in London voiced their concern over the possible development of "spin-off" drugs designed for healthy individuals seeking to raise their learning ability.

Dementia affects nearly three quarters of a million people in Britain alone, according to the Alzheimer's Disease Society. They say Alzheimer's is responsible for around half of these cases, and is on the increase.
Sufferers, mostly elderly people, often require full-time medical care which leaves families or state health services facing large medical bills.
McGaugh said some of the 200 compounds under examination could prove to be effective and safe in the near future, and this could cut down the number of patients in residential care.
Experts at the conference put the annual cost of treatment with such drugs at up to 1,500 pounds ($2,500), representing a significant saving on the cost of care in a nursing home.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has so far approved one drug (Tacrine) to treat Alzheimer patients, but it was found to be only modestly effective and had undesirable side-effects.
Alternatives are being developed by pharmaceutical companies world-wide, including SmithKline Beecham, Eli Lily and Sanofi.

A spokesman for the Ciba Foundation, a charity linked pharmaceutical company Ciba-Geigy, said they were more concerned with curing the ill than producing smart pills "for the worried well'. He said there was a move towards preventative drugs for dementia illnesses rather than searching for a cure.
But Steven Rose of the Brain and Behaviour research group at Milton Keynes University said potential cognitive enhancers could be in clinical trials within the next five years.
"If it happens with animals, why shouldn't it happen with humans?" said McGaugh, whose experiments with rats showed a clear improvement in long-term memory.

Scientists said although research was still in the early stages, with no experiments on humans to date, it was important to start raising the ethical and legal issues that would arise if smart drugs were to be developed for the general public.
Anthea Tinker of King's College, London, called for guidelines to be set up, warning that students could one day face pre-examination drug tests like athletes do now.

Scientists said further thought was needed on the implications of the drugs in both contexts. Some said doctors would face new challenges as they have never before had to gauge the level of a patient's decline in order to prescribe treatment.
In addition, the drugs have not been tested in conjunction with medication for heart disease and other age-related diseases.
If they are introduced, the drugs could also help victims of dementia resulting from Parkinson's disease, AIDS and even boxing injuries and pollution, the speakers said.
